content.text: React's API is small, but the front half of a .NET and React stack isn't: routing, server data, forms and the rendering model are yours to choose and learn. This path takes you from C# to a deployed ASP.NET Core and React app in eight stages, and plans months, not weeks, for the React side.

A .NET developer with a solid API budgets two weeks for "the React part". The first week goes well; then the bugs arrive. Switching customers quickly sometimes shows the previous customer's orders, typing in the search box refetches everything on each key, and a form loses what the user typed after a save. None of these needs a React API he hasn't seen. They come from the model: effects, state snapshots and caching server data.
The belief: React is a small library, so once the backend is done, the front end takes a few weeks.

Half of that is true. React's core really is small: components, props, state and a handful of hooks, and you can read the official Learn section in days. Compared with a full framework, there's less to memorize.

But React leaves the rest of the app to you. Its own docs say that starting without a framework means choosing your own tools for routing, data fetching and other common patterns, and they recommend a framework such as Next.js or React Router for new apps. Those choices, plus a mental model where rendering is a function of state and effects synchronize with the outside world, are the part that takes months.
A full-stack ASP.NET Core and React developer owns a feature across both halves:

items.text: The data model, the EF Core migration and the endpoint, with validation and authorization.
The API contract: shapes, status codes and error bodies the front end can rely on.
The React screens, with loading, empty and error states, and forms that survive a failed save.
Server data on the client: caching, refetching and invalidating after a change.
Tests and a pipeline that build, check and deploy both apps.

content.text: The stages from zero to senior

The ranges assume about 10 hours a week; more hours shorten them. Keep one project, for example a small invoicing app, and grow it through every stage. The path targets .NET 10, the LTS release supported until November 2028, and React 19.

content.text: Learning React's second edition came out in 2020, before React 19. Its chapters on components, hooks and functional JavaScript still hold, but anything React 19 added, and the current advice on data fetching and Server Components, is only on react.dev and nextjs.org: treat those as the main source. The two .NET books cover .NET 7 and EF Core 5; their core chapters hold, and Microsoft Learn has the newer APIs.

items.text: Budgeting weeks for the front end.
The library is small; the decisions around it aren't. Plan the React stages like the backend ones.
Fetching in effects by hand everywhere.
Without cancellation and caching, you get race conditions and stale screens. Use a server data library or a framework.
Copying every piece of server data into global state.
Server data is a cache of the database, not state you own.
Starting with Next.js before plain React.
You then can't tell React problems from framework problems.
If the API returns ProblemDetails, handle that one shape everywhere on the client.

content.text: Generate an OpenAPI document from the API and TypeScript types from it. Most bugs between the halves are a field renamed on one side only.

With Server Components or server rendering, Next.js runs on a server of its own. Next to ASP.NET Core, that means two deployments, two places to log and secure, and a choice about where each call happens. React's docs note that full-stack frameworks can also build single-page and static apps, so choose that mode on purpose.

items.text: One deployed app with a live URL and a README that explains how the front end talks to the API.
Tests on both sides running in CI, with the pipeline history visible.
A write-up of one hard bug, such as a race condition you fixed, with the before and after.
A clean history of small commits with clear messages.

React's API is small, but routing, server data, forms and the rendering model make the front half as big as the back.
Learn in order: C#, the API with auth, SQL with EF Core, the web platform and TypeScript, React, server data and Next.js, then testing and deployment.
Learn plain React before Next.js, and treat server data as a cache, not as state you own.
Target .NET 10 LTS and React 19, and use react.dev and nextjs.org as the main sources for the front end.
